title: How Teachers Unintentionally Encourage Cognitive Offloading
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky starts from what he sees while tutoring: students receive multiple complicated assignments per evening, often without notice, with unclear directions and study guides that do not match the tests. He argues that AI-era redesign should extend beyond the assignment to the conditions surrounding it, because students usually reach for AI not to cheat but to cope with situations beyond their control. He lists seven in-class offenders, including graded homework with too little modeling, missing background knowledge, overnight turnaround, ambiguous directions, mismatched study guides, product-only grading, and late feedback. Each gets a counter-move within the teacher's own course, paired with an honest note about the tension it creates, such as how much to scaffold or how lightly to grade process. He then turns to grade-level fixes like a shared assessment calendar, common grading and late-work practices, and protected common planning time. His conclusion is that AI literacy and assignment redesign are not enough without attention to the conditions of the work.
points: Potkalitsky reframes cognitive offloading as a rational response to pressure, ambiguity, thin background knowledge, and time scarcity rather than simple dishonesty.
Practical counter-moves include guided practice until students can start alone, a quick exit-ticket check before work goes home, and front-loading context and vocabulary for readings.
Directions written for a student working alone, including what to do when stuck, remove the most common reason to open a chatbot.
Grading process lightly alongside product, for example with completion credit and a single comment, lowers the risk of the final submission and the temptation to offload.
Some offenders are systemic, so grade-level teams need shared assessment calendars, aligned grading and absence practices, and leader-protected common planning time.
quotes: What if redesigning assignments in the age of AI is just one part of a larger redesign? What if the conditions surrounding an assignment matter more than the assignment itself?
Students don’t necessarily reach for AI to cheat or cognitively offload. They are simply trying to navigate a situation beyond their control.
If out-of-class work is practice, a student needs a rough version of the skill in order to engage effectively with that work.
Directions that answer “what do I do if I can’t start?” remove the most common reason to open a chatbot.
Study guides should be built from the test, after the test is written. Period.
When we grade process alongside product, we show students that both count. Grading the process also modulates the risk of the final submission.
Grade-level teams can agree on how many substantial out-of-class tasks students can tackle on a given evening, and share an assessment calendar that caps major assessments per day.
The goal is a classroom where students can succeed without a shortcut.
